questions.question: What is a pull request (PR) and why is it used?
questions.title: What Is a Pull Request?
questions.direct_answer: A pull request is a mechanism on hosting platforms like GitHub or GitLab to propose merging a feature branch into another branch, enabling code review, discussion, and automated checks before the merge happens. It's the gatekeeping step that ensures code quality and team alignment before changes reach production.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of professional team collaboration workflows — PRs are the gatekeeping mechanism for production code quality and team alignment.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing a PR purely as a technical merge operation without mentioning the human review process, discussion, and quality gates.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that PR descriptions and linked issues become part of the project's documentation and audit trail, helping future developers understand why decisions were made.

sections.title: Pull Requests as Team Gatekeepers
sections.content:
A **pull request** (PR) is a collaboration feature on platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket that sits between your feature branch and the target branch (usually main or develop).

Think of it as a checkpoint where your code gets inspected before entering the shared codebase — like airport security before boarding. When you open a PR, you're saying here's what I built, please review it before we merge. The platform creates a visual diff showing exactly what changed, line by line. Teammates can comment on specific lines, suggest improvements, and discuss trade-offs. Meanwhile, **automated checks** run in the background: tests, linters, security scans. The PR won't merge until reviewers approve and checks pass. This process catches bugs early, spreads knowledge across the team (everyone sees what's changing), and maintains a consistent code style. Without PRs, anyone could push broken code directly to main and crash production. PRs are the contract that says all code must be reviewed and validated before it affects real users.

sections.title: Creating and Reviewing a Pull Request Flow
When Pull Requests are Essential
sections.content: Use PRs for every change to shared branches in a professional team setting. This includes new features, bug fixes, refactoring, and even documentation updates. PRs are especially critical when multiple developers work on the same codebase — without them, conflicting changes and broken code slip through. They're also essential when code quality standards exist: your team uses linters, security scanners, or test coverage requirements that must pass before merge. Even solo developers benefit from PRs when working with open-source projects or creating a history trail for future reference. The only time you might skip a PR is for trivial changes on personal projects or true emergency hotfixes where the production system is down and every second counts — but even then, some teams require post-merge review PRs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with Pull Requests
sections.content:
- **Opening giant PRs**: Freshers often accumulate a week's worth of work (1000+ lines across 20 files) into one PR, making it nearly impossible to review thoroughly. Reviewers skim it, miss bugs, or delay indefinitely. Keep PRs focused on one feature or fix, ideally under 400 lines.
- **No description or context**: Pushing code with just the commit message and no PR description forces reviewers to dig through code to understand what changed and why. Always explain the problem being solved, the approach taken, and any trade-offs considered.
- **Ignoring CI failures**: Opening a PR with failing tests or linter errors and expecting reviewers to tell you what's wrong wastes everyone's time. Fix automated check failures before requesting review — treat red CI as a blocker.

sections.title: Key Points About Pull Requests
content: **Gatekeeping mechanism**: PRs prevent untested or unreviewed code from reaching production by requiring approval before merge
**Code review platform**: Enables line-by-line comments, discussions, and suggestions directly in the diff view
**Automated quality gates**: Integrates with CI/CD to run tests, linters, and security scans automatically on every PR
**Knowledge sharing**: Spreads understanding of code changes across the team since everyone can see and comment on PRs
**Audit trail**: PR descriptions, comments, and linked issues become permanent documentation of why decisions were made
**Merge strategies**: Platforms offer merge commit, squash, or rebase options affecting how history is recorded
**Approval workflow**: Teams configure rules like requiring 2 approvals or passing all checks before merge is allowed

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A pull request is how we propose changes to a shared codebase in a team environment. When I finish working on a feature branch, I don't merge it directly into main. Instead, I open a pull request on GitHub or GitLab, which creates a visual diff showing exactly what changed. The PR serves as a review checkpoint where teammates can comment on my code, suggest improvements, and catch bugs I might've missed. It's also where automated checks run — unit tests, code quality scans, security checks. All of those have to pass before the PR can merge. The key thing is that PRs aren't just technical — they're communication tools. The description I write explains what problem I'm solving and why I chose this approach. That context helps reviewers understand the change faster and makes the review more valuable. It also creates a permanent record in the project's history. Six months later, when someone asks why we implemented it this way, the PR has the full discussion captured. One mistake I've seen is treating PRs as just a formality and opening massive ones with no description. That makes reviewers' jobs really hard and slows everything down. Good PRs are focused, well-described, and have passing tests before you ask for review. That shows respect for your teammates' time and gets your code merged faster.

questions.question: What should you include in a pull request to make it easy to review?
questions.title: Pull Request Best Practices
questions.direct_answer: A good pull request includes a clear description explaining what changed and why, a linked issue or ticket number, a focused scope with minimal unrelated changes, passing automated tests, and relevant screenshots or examples. The goal is to make the reviewer's job as easy as possible, enabling fast, thorough review.

interviewer_intent.testing: Professional habits and empathy for reviewers — shows the candidate understands team dynamics and respects others' time during code review.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Opening a 2000-line PR with no description or mixing multiple unrelated features — this is a common junior habit that frustrates teams and delays reviews.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention self-reviewing your own PR before requesting review — catching your own typos, formatting issues, and obvious bugs first shows maturity and professionalism.

sections.title: Making PRs Easy to Review Accelerates Delivery
sections.content:
A pull request isn't just a code dump — it's a **communication package** designed to help reviewers understand your changes quickly and give valuable feedback. The reviewer is doing you a favor by spending their time on your code, so your job is to make that process as smooth as possible.

A well-crafted PR has a **clear description** that explains what problem you're solving and why you chose this approach (not just what files changed — Git already shows that). It includes a **linked issue number** like Fixes #234 so reviewers understand the business context without hunting through Jira. The scope is **focused** — one feature or one bug fix, not three unrelated things bundled together. All **automated checks pass** before you request review: tests green, linter happy, no merge conflicts. If the change affects UI, you include **screenshots or a demo video**. You've **self-reviewed** the diff to catch obvious mistakes like leftover debug prints or commented-out code. The PR description might even call out areas where you're uncertain and want specific feedback. This upfront effort pays off: reviewers can assess your work in 10 minutes instead of 40, they give better feedback because they understand the context, and your code merges faster.

sections.content:

sections.title: Example of a Well-Structured Pull Request
sections.content:
// PR Title: Add email validation for user registration (fixes #156)

// PR Description:
/*
### Problem
Users were registering with invalid email formats (e.g., "user@" or "@example.com"),
causing downstream errors in the email notification service.

### Solution
Added email validation in UserRegistrationService using Apache Commons Validator.
Rejects registration if email format is invalid, returns clear error message to client.

### Changes
- Added email validation method in UserRegistrationService
- Updated UserController to handle ValidationException
- Added 8 test cases covering valid/invalid email formats
- Updated API error response to include field-level error details

### Testing
All existing tests pass. New tests verify email validation logic.
Manually tested with invalid emails: "user@", "@domain.com", "notanemail"

### Screenshots
(Screenshot showing error message in UI when invalid email entered)

### Questions for Reviewers
Should we also validate email domain existence (DNS check)?
Or is format validation sufficient for now?
*/

// With this description, reviewers immediately understand context and can focus
// on code quality rather than figuring out what you're trying to accomplish

sections.title: Elements to Include in Your PRs
sections.content: Always include a **description** explaining the problem and your solution approach — even if it seems obvious to you, it might not be to reviewers unfamiliar with the feature. Link to the **issue or ticket number** using keywords like Fixes #123 or Closes #456 so the issue auto-closes when PR merges and reviewers can read full requirements. Keep **scope focused** on one logical change — if you fixed a bug and added a feature, split them into two PRs. Ensure **tests pass** and code builds before requesting review — red CI blocks should be fixed by you, not discovered by reviewers. Add **screenshots or videos** for any user-facing changes so reviewers can see the actual behavior without pulling your branch. Include **testing notes** describing what you tested and how, especially for edge cases. Call out **areas of uncertainty** where you want specific feedback, like I'm not sure if this caching strategy is optimal, would appreciate input. Finally, **self-review** the diff before submitting — you'll catch formatting issues, leftover debug code, and typos that would waste reviewers' time.

sections.title: Common PR Mistakes That Frustrate Reviewers
sections.content:
- **No description or context**: Opening a PR with just the commit message and no explanation of what problem you're solving forces reviewers to read all the code and guess your intent. Even worse is a one-word description like fixes. Always explain the why and how.
- **Massive scope with unrelated changes**: Mixing a bug fix, a new feature, and some refactoring into one 2000-line PR is overwhelming and delays review indefinitely. Reviewers don't have time to context-switch between three different problems. Keep PRs focused and under 400 lines when possible.
- **Requesting review with failing tests**: Pushing a PR with red CI and saying please review anyway wastes reviewers' time. They can't properly assess your code if tests are broken. Fix CI first, then request review.
- **Not self-reviewing first**: Many freshers hit create PR immediately after pushing code without looking at the diff themselves. You'd catch obvious mistakes like leftover console logs, formatting issues, or duplicate code if you spent two minutes reviewing your own changes first.

sections.title: Key Points for Easy-to-Review PRs
content: **Clear description**: explain the problem being solved and the solution approach, not just what files changed
**Linked issue**: use Fixes #123 to connect PR to ticket for context and auto-close issues on merge
**Focused scope**: one feature or one bug per PR, avoid mixing unrelated changes that require different mental contexts
**Passing tests**: ensure all CI checks pass before requesting review, treat red builds as blockers
**Screenshots or demos**: include visual proof of behavior for any user-facing changes to save reviewers from running code
**Self-review first**: review your own diff before requesting review to catch typos, debug code, and formatting issues
**Testing notes**: document what you tested and how, especially edge cases and error scenarios

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A good pull request is designed to make the reviewer's job as easy as possible. The first thing is a clear description that explains what problem I'm solving and why I chose this approach. I don't just say updated user service — I explain the business context like users were experiencing timeout errors during registration, so I added async processing to the email service. I also link to the issue number using Fixes #123 so reviewers can see the full requirements without leaving GitHub. The scope is focused on one thing. If I fixed a bug and added a feature, I'll split them into separate PRs because mixing them forces the reviewer to context-switch between different problems. I keep PRs under 400 lines when possible since big PRs rarely get thorough reviews. Before I request review, I make sure all the automated checks pass — tests, linters, everything green. If CI is failing, that's my job to fix, not the reviewer's job to point out. For anything that affects the UI, I include screenshots or a short video showing the behavior because that saves the reviewer from having to pull my branch and run the code themselves. One thing that really helps is self-reviewing my own PR first. I go through the diff line by line before requesting review and I almost always find things I missed — a leftover console log, a typo in a comment, formatting that's off. Catching those myself shows respect for the reviewer's time. Finally, if there's an area where I'm uncertain, I call it out explicitly in the description and ask for specific feedback. That makes the review more valuable for both of us.

questions.question: What is a draft pull request and when would you use it?
questions.title: Draft Pull Requests
questions.direct_answer: A draft pull request signals that the work is still in progress and not ready for formal review — it enables early feedback, visibility to the team, and CI checks without requesting a full review. Teams use it to get architectural input before investing heavily in implementation details.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of collaboration features and good team communication habits that prevent wasted work on wrong approaches.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing draft PRs exist and instead opening a regular PR with a title like WIP: don't merge yet, which clutters the review queue.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that draft PRs are great for getting early architectural feedback before investing in a full implementation — asking is this the right approach saves rework.

sections.title: Draft PRs for Early Feedback Without Formal Review
sections.content:
A **draft pull request** is a special PR state on GitHub and GitLab that signals this work is in progress and not ready for formal review yet. It shows up in the PR list with a Draft label and doesn't send review request notifications to your team.

The key benefit is **early visibility** — you can share your approach with the team while you're still building it, getting feedback on architecture and design decisions before you invest hours finishing every detail. Draft PRs also let you **run automated checks** like tests and linters on your in-progress code to catch issues early. You can push commits, see CI results, and discuss the approach in comments, but the PR clearly indicates don't review this thoroughly yet.

Think of it like showing someone a rough sketch before you paint the full picture — you want to confirm the composition is right before spending time on details. When you're ready for real review, you click Ready for review and the draft status is removed, triggering normal review workflows. This feature prevents the old anti-pattern of opening a regular PR titled WIP: don't merge, which clutters the review queue and confuses what actually needs attention. Draft PRs give you the collaboration benefits of a PR without creating noise for reviewers.

sections.title: Open a Draft PR, Then Mark It Ready
sections.content:
```bash
# Open a PR as a draft from the CLI (GitHub CLI)
git checkout -b feature/caching-layer
git commit -m "Sketch cache key strategy"
git push -u origin feature/caching-layer
gh pr create --draft --title "Caching layer (early feedback)" \
  --body "Validating the cache key approach before building it out."

# When the work is genuinely ready for review:
gh pr ready        # removes draft status, notifies reviewers
```

sections.title: Draft Pull Requests at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What a draft PR is|~Work-in-progress state|Draft label on GitHub|no review notifications|signals not ready
emerald|Early feedback|~Validate direction|architecture before details|ask is this right?|saves rework
amber|CI still runs|~Catch issues early|tests + linters execute|results on incomplete code|push commits freely
rose|Convert when ready|~Ready for review button|removes draft status|triggers normal review|replaces WIP: title hacks

sections.title: Step 1: Confirm Architectural Direction Early
sections.content: Use a draft PR when you want to validate your high-level approach before implementing everything. For example, you're adding a caching layer to a service and you've sketched out the cache key strategy and invalidation logic in 50 lines of code. You open a draft PR and ask the team does this approach make sense, or should I use a different cache key format? Getting this feedback early saves you from building 500 lines of code based on a flawed strategy. Senior developers appreciate being asked early rather than being handed a finished implementation that needs fundamental rework. Draft PRs for architectural review are especially valuable when you're working in unfamiliar parts of the codebase or making decisions that affect multiple teams.

sections.title: Step 2: Share Progress for Visibility and Collaboration
sections.content: Draft PRs help coordinate work when multiple people are touching related code. If you're refactoring a core service that other developers depend on, you can open a draft PR showing your changes and comment heads up, I'm restructuring the order service interface, let me know if this impacts your work. This prevents duplicate effort and merge conflicts later. Draft PRs also give your team visibility into what you're working on during longer features — instead of disappearing into a branch for a week, you push incremental commits to a draft PR so teammates can see progress and jump in with suggestions. Some teams use draft PRs to run CI checks on experimental code or proof-of-concept work before deciding whether to proceed with the feature.

sections.title: Common Draft PR Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Leaving PRs in draft forever**: Freshers sometimes open a draft PR and forget to mark it ready for review when it's actually complete, causing confusion about whether the work is done. When your code is ready, convert it immediately.
- **Using WIP prefix instead of draft**: Before draft PRs existed, teams used conventions like WIP: add user service or DO NOT MERGE in PR titles. Now that draft is a built-in feature, use it instead of title hacks — it's cleaner and integrates with platform workflows.
- **Opening draft PRs for minor work**: If you're fixing a small bug or making a trivial change, just finish it and open a regular PR. Draft PRs are for cases where you genuinely need early feedback or visibility on incomplete work, not every single task.

sections.title: Key Points About Draft Pull Requests
content: **Work-in-progress signal**: clearly marks PR as not ready for formal review, preventing reviewers from spending time on incomplete code
**Early feedback**: enables you to get architectural or design input before investing heavily in implementation details
**CI checks still run**: automated tests and quality checks execute on draft PRs just like regular PRs for early issue detection
**Team visibility**: shows teammates what you're working on without formally requesting their review time
**Convert to ready**: when code is complete, mark draft as ready for review to trigger normal review workflow and notifications
**Better than WIP titles**: replaces old convention of WIP: or DO NOT MERGE in titles with a proper platform feature
**Collaboration enabler**: prevents wasted work by surfacing conflicts or duplicate efforts early in development

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A draft pull request is a feature on GitHub that lets you open a PR that's clearly marked as not ready for review yet. It shows up with a Draft label and doesn't send review notifications to your team. The main reason to use it is to get early feedback before you've finished implementing everything. For example, let's say I'm adding a caching layer to a service. I've got the basic structure in place and I want to check with my team that I'm using the right cache key strategy before I build out all the edge cases and tests. I'll open a draft PR with that initial code and ask hey, does this approach look right? That way, if someone spots a problem with my approach, I haven't wasted a bunch of time going down the wrong path. Draft PRs also help with visibility. If I'm working on a longer feature that's gonna take a few days, I can open a draft and push commits as I go. My teammates can see what I'm building and jump in if they have suggestions or if my work conflicts with something they're doing. The platform still runs all the automated checks on draft PRs — tests, linters, everything. So I can catch issues early even though the code isn't ready for human review yet. When I've finished the implementation and I'm ready for actual review, I click the button to mark it ready for review. Then it becomes a normal PR and sends notifications to reviewers. The alternative people used before draft PRs existed was opening a regular PR with a title like WIP: don't merge yet, but that clutters the review queue and it's not as clean as using the built-in draft feature.

questions.question: How do you address review comments on a pull request?
questions.title: Addressing Pull Request Review Comments
questions.direct_answer: Address review comments by making the requested code changes in your local branch, committing them with a descriptive message, and pushing to the same branch — this automatically updates the pull request. Then respond to each comment in the PR thread explaining what you changed or providing context if you disagree. Clear communication keeps the review process moving smoothly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands code review as a collaborative conversation, not just a checklist — testing both Git workflow knowledge and professional communication skills.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Pushing fixes without responding to comments, leaving the reviewer to hunt through new commits trying to figure out what changed and whether their feedback was addressed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that you treat each comment as a learning opportunity and sometimes schedule a quick call with the reviewer if the feedback involves architectural decisions — showing you value human discussion over just text threads.

sections.title: The Pull Request Review Cycle
sections.content:
Addressing review comments is a **collaborative process** where you respond to feedback from teammates who've reviewed your code changes. When someone reviews your pull request, they might suggest improvements, ask questions about your approach, or point out potential bugs. Your job is to **acknowledge each comment**, make the necessary changes, and communicate what you did. This isn't about blindly accepting every suggestion — it's a **technical conversation** where both sides learn. The beauty of Git's branch model is that every commit you push to your feature branch automatically appears in the open PR, so reviewers see updates in real-time without you creating a new PR.

Think of it like editing a shared Google Doc — your changes show up immediately for collaborators. Good communication during this phase builds trust with your team and demonstrates professional maturity that employers value highly.

sections.title: Addressing Review Comments
sections.content:
blue|Make the change|~In your branch|edit, then commit|a clear message per review|push to the same branch
emerald|PR updates itself|~No new PR needed|same branch -> PR refreshes|reviewers see it live|like a shared doc
amber|Reply to every comment|~Close the loop|Fixed in abc123|disagree? explain politely|resolve conversations
rose|Avoid force-push mid-review|~Don't lose comments|rebase only if needed|announce it first|keeps the diff sane

sections.title: Addressing Review Comments Workflow
When and How to Respond
sections.content: **Respond to every comment** even if it's just "Done" or "Fixed in commit abc123" — silence makes reviewers wonder if you saw their feedback. **Make changes immediately** when the feedback is clearly correct (like a bug or typo), but **ask clarifying questions** if you don't understand the suggestion before making changes. **Push back respectfully** when you disagree with a suggestion by explaining your reasoning with concrete trade-offs: "I kept the method inline because it's only called once and extracting it would make the flow harder to follow — but I'm open to changing it if you feel strongly." **Group related changes** into a single commit rather than making 10 micro-commits for each comment — this keeps the Git history readable. **Request a call** if the comment thread gets long or touches architectural decisions — a 10-minute discussion often resolves what would take 20 comments.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Silent fixing**: Pushing commits that address feedback without replying to the comments, forcing the reviewer to re-read all your code and guess what changed. Reviewers have limited time and this wastes it — always link your changes back to specific comments.
- **Defensive arguing**: Treating every suggestion as criticism and writing paragraphs defending your original approach instead of considering if the reviewer has a valid point. Code review isn't personal — it's about improving the code.
- **Force-pushing carelessly**: Using git push --force on a PR branch after someone has started reviewing, which can lose their draft comments or confuse the diff view. If you must rebase, communicate it clearly in the PR thread first.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Same branch updates PR**: Pushing new commits to your feature branch automatically updates the open pull request — no need to close and recreate it.
**Respond to every comment**: Acknowledge each piece of feedback with what you changed or why you disagree — silence creates uncertainty for reviewers.
**Commit messages matter**: Write clear commit messages like 'Extract validation method per review' so reviewers can track what changed without digging through diffs.
**Respectful disagreement is okay**: Code review is a conversation — if you have good reasoning for an approach, explain it rather than blindly accepting every suggestion.
**Mark comments resolved**: After addressing feedback, use GitHub/GitLab's 'Resolve conversation' feature to help reviewers track what's done.
**Group related fixes**: Make one commit for related changes rather than 10 micro-commits — keeps Git history clean and reviewable.
**Avoid force-push during review**: Force-pushing rewrites history and can confuse reviewers or lose their draft comments — communicate before rebasing.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When I get review comments on a pull request, I treat it as a conversation, not a checklist. First, I read through all the comments to understand the full scope of what needs changing. Then I make the requested changes locally in my feature branch — things like adding validation, fixing typos, or refactoring methods. Once I've made the changes, I commit them with a clear message like 'Add null checks and extract validation method per review' so it's obvious what I did. Then I push to the same branch, which automatically updates the pull request. The key part is I don't just push silently — I go back to each comment in the PR thread and respond. I might say 'Fixed in commit abc123' or 'Good catch, updated the method signature at line 42.' If I disagree with a suggestion, I explain my reasoning respectfully, like 'I kept this logic inline because it's only used once and extracting it would make the flow harder to follow, but I'm open to changing it if you feel strongly.' One mistake I've learned to avoid is force-pushing during an active review because it can lose the reviewer's draft comments or mess up the diff view. If I need to rebase, I mention it in the PR thread first. I also mark conversations as resolved after addressing them so reviewers can easily see what's done. The goal is to make the reviewer's job easy — they took time to help improve my code, so clear communication shows I respect that effort.

questions.question: What are the different merge strategies available when merging a pull request on GitHub?
questions.title: PR Merge Strategies: Merge, Squash, Rebase
questions.direct_answer: GitHub offers three merge strategies: Merge commit creates a merge commit preserving all branch history, Squash and merge combines all PR commits into a single commit with a clean message, and Rebase and merge replays commits linearly without creating a merge commit. Each has different trade-offs for history readability and auditability.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical workflow knowledge — this comes up in daily work discussions and team code review practices where strategy choice affects repository history.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing the basic merge exists — not realizing squash is the most popular choice for keeping main branch history clean and readable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain which strategy suits which team philosophy — squash for clean main, rebase for linear history purists, merge commit for full auditability and traceability.

sections.title: Three Ways to Merge and Their Impact
sections.content:
When you're ready to merge a pull request on GitHub, you choose from three **merge strategies** that fundamentally change how the commit history looks. **Merge commit** creates a special merge commit that ties your feature branch back into main, preserving every commit you made on the branch — this keeps full traceability but can clutter history with work-in-progress commits like fix typo or forgot semicolon. **Squash and merge** takes all your feature branch commits and combines them into one clean commit on main with a polished message — this is like summarizing a conversation instead of recording every sentence.

The main branch stays readable, but you lose the detailed step-by-step history. **Rebase and merge** replays your commits one by one on top of main without creating a merge commit, resulting in a perfectly linear history as if you wrote the code directly on main — it's the cleanest timeline but loses the branch context entirely.

Think of it like editing a movie: merge commit keeps all the raw footage, squash creates a highlight reel, and rebase makes it look like one continuous take. Different teams prefer different strategies based on whether they value detailed audit trails or clean, scannable history.

sections.title: How Each Strategy Affects Git History
Choosing the Right Strategy for Your Team
sections.content:
Use **squash and merge** when you want main branch history to be a clean, readable timeline of features and fixes — this is the most popular choice in modern teams because git log on main shows one commit per PR with a clear description. It's ideal when developers make lots of small work-in-progress commits during development.

Use **merge commit** when you need full auditability and traceability of every change, often required in regulated industries like finance or healthcare where you must prove exactly when and how each line changed. Also use it when branch context matters — seeing which commits were developed together as part of one feature.

Use **rebase and merge** when your team values a perfectly linear history and developers already write clean, well-structured commits on feature branches. It's popular in open-source projects where contributors are expected to craft good commit messages before submitting PRs.

sections.title: Common Merge Strategy Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using merge commit with messy branch history**: Freshers often use the default merge commit strategy without realizing it imports all their fix typo, oops forgot import, actually fix it this time commits into main, creating noise that makes git log unusable. If you're making frequent WIP commits, use squash instead.
- **Squashing when commit-level detail matters**: Some teams need to see the detailed progression of changes for compliance or debugging — squashing destroys that granularity. Understand your team's audit requirements before choosing.
- **Rebasing public branches**: If multiple people are working on a branch and you rebase it, you rewrite history and force everyone else to deal with conflicts. Rebase is safe for personal feature branches only, never for shared branches.

sections.title: Key Points About Merge Strategies
content: **Merge commit**: preserves full branch history with all original commits visible, creates explicit merge commit showing branch integration point
**Squash and merge**: combines all PR commits into one clean commit on main, ideal for keeping main branch history readable and scannable
**Rebase and merge**: replays commits linearly without merge commit, creates appearance that work was done directly on main branch
**History readability**: squash produces cleanest main branch timeline, merge commit shows full detail, rebase gives linear progression
**Auditability trade-off**: merge commit keeps complete record of when changes were made, squash loses individual commit timestamps
**Team convention**: most teams standardize on one strategy and enforce it via GitHub branch protection rules
**Commit message matters**: with squash, the final commit message is crucial since it's the only one that appears in main history

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: GitHub gives you three ways to merge a pull request, and they each affect the commit history differently. The first is merge commit, which is the default. It creates a special merge commit that ties your feature branch back into main while keeping all your individual commits visible. So if you made five commits on your branch, all five show up in the main history plus the merge commit. That's great for auditability because you can see every step, but it can make the history messy if you have a lot of work-in-progress commits like fix typo. The second option is squash and merge, which is probably the most popular. It takes all your commits and combines them into one clean commit on main with a nice summary message. The main branch stays really readable — each commit represents one PR or one feature. The downside is you lose the detailed step-by-step history of how you built it. The third is rebase and merge, which replays your commits one by one on top of main without creating a merge commit. You get a perfectly linear history that looks like you wrote everything directly on main. It's the cleanest timeline, but you lose the context of which commits belonged to which feature branch. Most teams pick one strategy and stick with it. Squash is popular because main branch history stays clean and readable. Merge commit is used when you need full audit trails for compliance. And rebase is favored by teams that want that perfectly linear look.
